How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Mexico, are appealing a decision by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated January 15, 2020, rejecting their refugee protection claims on the ground that there would be an internal flight alternative (IFA) for them in Mexico City, in the capital, Pachuca (state of Hidalgo), or Tlaxcala (state of Tlaxcala) if they were to return to their country.

The appellants allege that they are threatened by Mexican society as a whole due to their sexual orientation. They also claim to have been threatened with death on several occasions by a man named XXXX, a drug dealer who wanted to sell his products to customers at XXXX XXXX where Mr. XXXX worked in Mérida (state of Yucatan).
On XXXX XXXX, 2018, the appellants left Mexico for Canada. They filed their refugee protection claim on June 27, 2018.

The RPD concluded that the appellants are indeed a couple, that their sexual orientation is homosexual, that their testimony was generally credible, with the exception of the problems they allegedly had with XXXX, that they were discriminated against in their country but that these unfortunate experiences do not constitute persecution, even cumulatively. The RPD concluded that there is no serious possibility of persecution due to their sexual orientation, nor is there a risk regarding the identified agent of risk, and that it would be objectively reasonable for them to relocate to one of the three proposed IFAs.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) rendered an initial decision on January 27, 2021. The appellants filed an application to reopen on January 29, 2021, noting that new evidence supporting their claims, filed on October 1, 2020, had not been processed. The reopening was authorized on March 4, 2021, and the file was referred to a differently constituted panel.
The appellants submitted 10 new pieces of evidence and a request for an oral hearing. The new evidence is partially admitted, but the request for an oral hearing is denied.

In their memorandum, the appellants contest the RPD's conclusions regarding the first prong of the IFA, which represents the sole determinative issue on appeal. They argue that they cannot safely relocate to any of the proposed cities because they will be persecuted by reason of their sexual orientation everywhere in the country.
Like the RPD, the RAD considered Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression when rendering its decision.

The appeals are dismissed. The RPD correctly determined that the appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. PARTIAL ADMISSION OF NEW EVIDENCE AND DENIAL OF REQUEST FOR AN ORAL HEARING

To be admissible by the RAD, the new evidence must first meet the criteria under subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and then those in Singh,1 adapted from Raza,2 both from the Federal Court of Appeal. Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA states that "the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection." The Court has held that three admissibility criteria in Raza, namely credibility, relevance and newness, also apply to any request to admit new evidence before the RAD.

The appellants submitted new evidence in support of their refugee protection claim when perfecting their appeal record in February 2020: * A-1: Three news articles dated October and November 2019 reporting discrimination, particularly against those whose sexual orientation is not heterosexual.

This exhibit is not admitted on appeal because it does not meet the criteria contained in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA as it involves facts that occurred before the RPD's decision was signed. The appellants did not explain why these documents would not have been reasonably available, nor did they explain the circumstances that prevented their submission to the RPD. Despite the lack of an explanation, the RAD conducted its own assessment of these criteria and concluded that these articles were reasonably available and that no circumstances were in place to prevent their submission to the RPD.

The appellants then submitted nine additional documents as new evidence, dated October 1, 2020: * A-2: A letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX dated August 29, 2020; * A-3: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Javier Found, Young Man Missing From CDMX Burned in Cuernavaca," dated August 25, 2020; * A-4: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Javier Burned, Wrapped in LGBT+ Flag, Found in Cuernavaca," dated August 25, 2020; * A-5: Article from the Human Rights Commission in Mexico City, dated July 2, 2020; * A-6: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Organizations Reveal Tlaxcala Without Instructions to Eradicate Sexual Orientation Discrimination," dated May 17, 2020; * A-7: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Faced With an Epidemic, Demands for Guaranteed Rights for the LGBT Community," dated May 20, 2020; * A-8: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Call to Address Discrimination Against the LGBT Community in Work Centres," dated June 27, 2020; * A-9: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Hateful Homicide because of LGBT Phobia in Mexico," dated May 2, 2020; * A-10: A newspaper article titled [translation] "Homophobic Hate Crimes in Mexico Without Official Statistics," dated May 2, 2020.

In order to be admissible before the RAD, this new evidence submitted following the perfection of the appeal record must first meet the criteria of subrule 29(4) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules. When deciding whether to allow or dismiss a request to submit new evidence after the deadline, the RAD must consider a) the document's relevance and probative value; b) any new evidence the document brings to the proceedings; c) whether the party, with reasonable effort, could have transmitted the document with the appeal record.

The RPD rendered its decision on January 15, 2020. Exhibits A-2 to A-10 are all dated after the decision and, a priori, could not have been submitted, as they all involve events that occurred after the RPD's decision was rendered. They all present facts relating to the appellants' fear of persecution by reason of their sexual orientation which, according to the RAD, is relevant. The RAD therefore concludes that the criteria in subrule 29(4) of the RAD Rules have been met.

All of these exhibits also meet the criteria in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA in that they are all dated after the RPD's decision and could not reasonably have been submitted earlier because they report facts that occurred after the RPD's decision was signed. The RAD must therefore establish whether these exhibits are credible, relevant and new, in accordance with the case law.

There is no reason to question the credibility of the documents presented, which include an affidavit, an official report from the Human Rights Commission in Mexico City, along with press clippings from official and local newspapers. The documents as a whole present new facts relating to the murder of a homosexual activist and the discriminatory experience of those with diverse sexual orientations in Mexico City, Pachuca and Tlaxcala. Given the content of these documents and the appellants' allegations of persecution by reason of their sexual orientation, the RAD considers these documents relevant.
Exhibits A-2 to A-10 are admitted into evidence under this appeal.

However, the RAD is of the opinion that the new evidence does not meet the criteria of subsection 110(6) of the IRPA and does not allow for an oral hearing to be held. In order to hold a hearing, the cumulative criteria of subsection 110(6) of the IRPA must be met, namely that the new evidence admitted raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. The appellants' credibility is not at stake, these documents are relevant but not essential to this appeal and would not, on their own, justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claims in this case. The request for an oral hearing is dismissed.

In accordance with Huruglica,3 the RAD conducted an independent review of all the evidence on the record, which included listening to the hearing in this case, and applied the correctness standard since the RPD did not have a meaningful advantage regarding the issue of credibility.

The appellants raise two grounds for appeal. First, they consider that the RPD erred in its analysis of section 96 of the IRPA and, second, that it erred in its analysis of the documentary evidence regarding the proposed IFA cities. In the RAD's view, this appeal only involves the issue of the IFA in the cities of Mexico City, Pachuca or Tlaxcala.

It is important to first note that the existence of an IFA is assessed on the basis of a two-pronged test to determine whether there is a place elsewhere in the country where the claimant, in this case the appellant, would not have a well-founded fear of persecution or would not be subjected to a risk under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA4 and, considering all of the circumstances, whether it would be objectively reasonable for the claimant to settle there.5

In Olusola v. Canada, Justice McHaffie describes the framework of analysis and the burden of proof with respect to an IFA in the following terms: [8] To determine if a viable IFA exists, the RAD must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that (1) the claimant will not be subject to persecution (on a "serious possibility" standard), or a section 97 danger or risk (on a "more likely than not" standard) in the proposed IFA; and (2) in all the circumstances, including circumstances particular to the claimant, conditions in the IFA are such that it would not be unreasonable for the claimant to seek refuge there: Thirunavukkarasu, at pages 595 to 597; Hamdan v. Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2017 FC 643, at paras. 10 to 12.6 The Refugee Protection Division did not err in its analysis of the first prong of the internal flight alternative

When assessing the first prong of the IFA under the legal argument in section 96 of the IRPA, the panel must analyze the factors of the agent of persecution's ability to locate the claimant, as well as the former's motivation to do so. Justice McHaffie of the Federal Court distinguishes these concepts with the following: It is important to note that there is a difference between a persecutor's ability to pursue an individual throughout a country and his desire to do so or interest in doing so. The fact that a persecutor is able to pursue an individual is not decisive evidence that he is motivated to do so. If the persecutor has no desire to find, pursue and/or persecute an individual, or interest in doing so, it is reasonable to conclude that there is no serious possibility of persecution.7

Thus, while the agent of persecution's ability to act, an important but not decisive factor, rests primarily on evidence of past action, which therefore demands the application of the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities, establishing the agent of persecution's motivation requires a burden of proof of serious possibility, because here this is an assessment of future risk that a claimant would face should they return to the country. Upon completing this analysis, the decision-maker should conclude the first prong of the IFA study by answering the initial question, that is, whether the claimant would face a serious possibility of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, with consideration for the analysis regarding the agent of persecution's ability and motivation.

Here, the appellants identified an agent of persecution, namely XXXX, and identified a risk due to the country's insecurity and the homophobic behaviour of Mexican society as a whole. XXXXability to act and interest

In their testimony, both appellants stated that although XXXXwent after them, his behaviour had more to do with the fact that he was banned from selling drugs than it did with their sexual orientation. The RPD nonetheless sought to find out why the latter would attempt to track them down in the three proposed cities. They stated that he was seeking vengeance. When asked to identify what methods XXXXmight use to locate them, the appellants stated that he certainly had the means, but did not have the knowledge.

The RPD noted that neither XXXXnor any accomplice tracked down the appellants when they travelled to Chiquila, Holbox or Cancún over several months, locations where they worked and where they were able to meet, shop and go to the beach together. Ultimately, they did not live in hiding in these locations. XXXXdid not attempt to reach them through their family or friend. The RPD noted that the only time XXXXlocated the appellants was when they returned to Mérida with the belief that he had forgotten them.

In their memorandum, the appellants state that XXXXis [translation] "a powerful drug trafficker in their city."8 But he also claims that he was banned from several bars in the city.9 In the RAD's view, he is either a powerful figure who rules the city, or a drug dealer that several bar owners can ban without hesitation.

From its own analysis of the evidence regarding XXXXand any accomplices, the RAD isp-,[.;======[,l; of the opinion that the RPD's conclusion that the appellants failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, their inability to safely relocate to Mexico City, Pachuca or Tlaxcala is correct. It has not been established that XXXXwould have the means or the interest to go after them in these three cities. The insecurity experienced in Mexico

During their hearing, the appellants also stated their fear relating to the insecurity in Mexico. Relying on the evidence contained in the National Documentation Package (NDP) on Mexico, the RPD acknowledged a situation of impunity and violence throughout the Mexican territory, which has consequences for the entire population. The RPD therefore concluded that appellants would be [translation] "in the same situation as all other Mexican citizens who are subjected to the same risk in Mexico."10 In the RPD's view, the appellants would ultimately face a generalized and non-personalized risk if they returned to their country.

In their memorandum, the appellants state that the RPD erred because its reasoning in this regard was tainted by a significant error, that is, the fact that this conclusion [translation] "replaces objective evidence with hypothetical deductions."11

The RAD reviewed the RPD's conclusion and draws the same conclusion. The RPD relied on both the appellants' testimony and the objective evidence in the NDP on Mexico and concluded that there is, indeed, an endemic problem of violence in Mexico that often goes unpunished, resulting in a generalized insecurity that is felt by the entire population. No deduction or assumption was made by the RPD here, but rather a conclusion based on the evidence on the record.

From its own analysis of the evidence regarding insecurity, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD's conclusion that the appellants failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, their inability to safely relocate to Mexico City, Pachuca or Tlaxcala is correct. Discrimination by Mexican society

According to the appellants, Mexican society is such that they will be persecuted due to their sexual orientation no matter where they attempt to relocate. They testified at the hearing and report in their memorandum that they have faced several situations of discrimination in their lives, including situations involving employment and housing, that they have been intimidated and insulted because of their sexual orientation, and that they have been physically assaulted.12

The RPD concluded that, although the appellants faced several instances of discrimination and violence due to their sexual orientation, these incidents, even cumulatively, do not amount to persecution in this case. Despite recognizing their membership in the particular social group of Mexican homosexual men, the appellants failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution due to their sexual orientation.

The analysis of any refugee protection claim is prospective and the first prong of the IFA analysis requires a study of the serious possibility of persecution in the event of relocation to the proposed cities, in this case, Mexico City, Pachuca and Tlaxcala.

The RPD extensively reviewed the documentary evidence in the NDP on Mexico and concluded that the three proposed cities are safe for the appellants. The appellants state that the new evidence presented and admitted on appeal points to different conclusions regarding the safety situation of homosexual men in Mexico.

It is important to note that both the documentary evidence in the NDP on Mexico, along with the new evidence presented by the appellants, show that there is indeed discrimination against those with a sexual orientation other than heterosexual in Mexico, including homosexual men.13 According to the National Council for the Prevention of Discrimination, "discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity continues to be a structural phenomenon with extensive social roots..." According to a representative of the Executive Commission of Attention to Victims, crimes against sexual minorities are constant and usually driven by prejudice. According to a 2016 survey of 425 members of the LGBT community, 7 out of 10 have experienced discrimination in a school setting and 5 out of 10 have experienced harassment or discrimination in the workplace. This discrimination reportedly stems from the influence of the Catholic religion. In a 2014 survey of 2,669 people, 87% identified as Catholic and 59% declared their support for same-sex marriage.14

But there has also been a clear improvement in the living conditions of those who belong to this particular social group. The Mexican Supreme Court concluded that the country's Constitution obligates every authority to fight against discrimination based on sexual orientation, while federal laws, and occasionally state laws, seek to prevent and eliminate discrimination in this regard. Those with diverse sexual orientations have the ability to form associations, as the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association (ILGA) exists in Mexico. The association has identified at least 20 of 32 states with laws prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, including Mexico City and Tlaxcala. These laws, however, do not provide victims with specific safeguards. In a 2017 report, the same association states that employment discrimination is a criminal act. A Mexican researcher and activist confirmed that laws intended to protect sexual minorities are partially effective and that changes are noticeable throughout society due to campaigning, television shows and private company support for the rights of people with diverse sexual orientations. Same-sex marriage is also permitted in at least 11 states, while Mexico's Supreme Court declared unconstitutional any law that prohibits same-sex marriage. According to the director of Investigaciones Queer, A.C. [Queer Research], open cities exist where those from the LBGT community feel safe from abuse, even though police officers may go after them.15

One researcher offered this summary: [t]here is still a lot of discrimination and violence towards the LGBT community, particularly in small cities and rural areas. Things have been improving in the last few years, [for example,] more than 80 cities now have a gay parade and there is a growing LGBT movement across the country but at the same time, many sector[s] in society are still very conservative. (Researcher 3 June 2017) ... there are many cities that are quite friendly such as Mexico City, Guadalajara, Tijuana, Cancun and Acapulco. There are gay clubs and bars in most of the cities across the country but again, that doesn't mean that there's no violence against [the LGBTI] community (Researcher 3 June 2017).16

Regarding the cities of Tlaxcala and Pachuca in particular, the RPD's analysis of their safety was brief. It noted that both cities are located in fairly peaceful states. The evidence in the NDP on Mexico is also limited, if not non-existent.

The appellants submitted Exhibit A-6, a newspaper article from a local Mexican media outlet dated May 17, 2020, titled "Organizations Reveal Tlaxcala Without Instructions to Eradicate Sexual Orientation Discrimination." According to the appellants, this article demonstrates that discrimination has not yet been [translation] "eradicated," nor has persecution on the basis of sexual orientation, notably because same-sex marriage is not permitted, hate-motivated killings are not punishable and conversion therapies are not prohibited.

Reading this exhibit, it is clear that legislators in the state of Tlaxcala attempted to pass a law allowing same-sex marriage, but it is lagging. They did, however, pass a law recognizing the identity of trans people and amended the civil code accordingly. It also states that the activities planned for the international day against homophobia were cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Ultimately, this article speaks of the Tlaxcala state authorities' progress and slowness in the fight against homophobia and the protection of those with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity or expression.

The appellants submitted Exhibit A-7, an article from a local Mexican newspaper dated May 20, 2020, titled "Faced With an Epidemic, Demands for Guaranteed Rights for the LGBT Community." According to the appellants, this article demonstrates that discrimination and persecution on the basis of sexual orientation still occur in the state of Hidalgo, where Pachuca is located. Members of the LGBT community are allegedly denied their right to access health care and this violation has been exacerbated under the COVID-19 pandemic. Hate crimes against members of this community reportedly go unpunished.

This article reports on the steps taken by the civil organization Juntos por Hidlago [Together for Hidalgo] with local authorities, noting that the COVID-19 pandemic exacerbates the vulnerability of members of the LGBT community, particularly in terms of health care. A representative of the organization states that [translation] "this group of people faces greater stigma because of the virus, as well as new barriers when seeking medical care," thus justifying their call for non-discrimination of members of this community and a review of sexual diversity laws and policies. The article concludes with a reminder that only 14 Mexican states have passed laws qualifying crimes against persons from that community as hate crimes.

This article is brief, to say the least, since the reader is given no concrete examples to clarify the situation reported. It contains grand statements without facts to support them. In the opinion of this representative of an organization that defends the rights of members of the LGBT community, the right to health is being compromised, particularly during a pandemic, but there is nothing to elucidate this statement.

In the RAD's view, these two articles offer a mixed picture of the situation in the states of Tlaxcala and Hidalgo. We learn that organizations defending the rights of members of the LGBT community are allowed to exist, act, speak out and challenge the authorities, that activities intended to promote the fight against homophobia are organized annually, but that these have been cancelled or postponed due to the pandemic, not homophobia. These two articles also reveal that discrimination has not been "eradicated," but that measures are being put in place and laws are being adopted in this regard, despite sometimes slow progress in this regard.

The appellants also submitted exhibits A-2 to A-4, which involve the murder of an LGBT activist in Mexico City, Exhibit A-5, a report from the Human Rights Commission in Mexico City, and Exhibit A-10, a newspaper article that addresses the problems associated with compiling hate crimes against the LGBT community in Mexico City.

According to the appellants, these exhibits call into question the safe nature of Mexico City. More specifically, the appellants argue that they demonstrate the absence of [translation] "areas open to homosexual individuals" (paragraph 41 of the RPD's decision), that hate crimes are current (paragraph 42 of the RPD's decision), and that they are not properly accounted for, consequently undermining the RPD's conclusion that few people with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity or expression are murdered (paragraph 51 of the RPD's decision).

The RAD agrees with the appellants regarding the poor quality of statistics surrounding hate crimes and general crimes committed against those with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. This is evident from exhibits A-5 and A-10, as well as from the documentary evidence. As state laws are not always clear on how to record criminal motivation, these crimes are not always properly recorded. Moreover, these crimes are not widely reported to the authorities. There is no doubt that the statistics are not reliable.

The RPD stated that hate crimes against homosexual individuals are rarely discussed in Mexico City. The appellants submitted evidence that the gruesome murder of a homosexual leader did, in fact, occur in 2020. The RAD is of the opinion that, however unfortunate this event, and considering the poor quality of the statistics mentioned above, it remains unique.

The RAD does not agree with the appellants regarding the "areas open to homosexual individuals." Reading the documentary evidence, one concludes that they do exist, but that life inside these areas is not perfect, especially in Mexico City.

Here, in the RAD's view, homosexual men like the appellants continue to face discrimination in Mexico City, Pachuca and Tlaxcala, especially in terms of employment, housing and health. But it is also clear from the evidence in both the NDP and in the appellants' record that such discrimination does not amount to persecution, even when the facts are added together. On the contrary, Mexican authorities are working to improve the situation of these people, who are able to form associations, publicly demand respect for their rights, benefit from a national observatory on the hate crimes perpetrated against them, along with dedicated health centres, anti-discrimination laws, and so on. The appellants were able to work in several locations, even with the public, and were able to find housing on several occasions. Of course, this was not without problems. Ultimately, while discrimination has not been eradicated, there is no reason to speak of persecution here.17 Based on the documentary evidence reviewed above, the situation of those with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity or gender appears to have improved, particularly in Mexico City.

In conclusion, while the RAD is sympathetic to the appellants' situation, it is of the opinion that the RPD's conclusion that the appellants failed to demonstrate a serious possibility of persecution by reason of their sexual orientation in Mexico City, Pachuca or Tlaxcala is correct. For all the above reasons, these cities are safe locations for the appellants. The Refugee Protection Division did not err in its analysis of the second prong of the internal flight alternative

The RPD asked the appellants why it would not be reasonable for them to relocate to Mexico City, Pachuca or Tlaxcala. They reiterated that they fear for their lives everywhere in the country and that they seek to live openly as homosexual individuals. They did not point out any particular difficulties relating to their profile. The RPD noted that both are fluent in Spanish, have work experience despite the difficulties experienced, are educated and have no particular physical problems. In addition to the documentary evidence previously considered, the RPD concluded that the appellants failed to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that it would be objectively unreasonable for them to relocate to the proposed cities.
The appellants did not challenge the RPD's conclusions regarding this second prong of the IFA, save for a brief mention relating to their profile.18

The RAD reviewed this conclusion by the RPD in light of all the evidence on the record and reached the same conclusion. Here, the RAD notes that, in the past, the appellants were able to work in several locations, even with the public, find housing despite certain difficulties, frequent public places together, but not without encountering reluctance from people regarding their homosexuality. The appellants have therefore not established that they would experience excessive difficulties if they returned to Mexico City, Pachuca or Tlaxcala. Conclusion regarding the internal flight alternative

The RAD concludes that the appellants have not established a serious possibility of persecution pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA if they returned to Mexico City, Pachuca or Tlaxcala, or that relocation to these cities would be unreasonable for them.

In conclusion, the appellants failed to establish that they would face a serious possibility of persecution if they returned to Mexico, or that they would be subjected personally, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, a risk to their lives, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the appeals are dismissed and the RPD's determination that the appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA is confirmed.
